No — both fail under the GDPR.

- Recital 32 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 states that consent must be a clear affirmative act, and that silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not constitute consent — so the pre-ticked box is invalid [2].
- Article 7(3) gives the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time, and it must be as easy to withdraw as to give consent — a signed-letter-only rule does not meet that standard [4].
- Withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing before withdrawal, and the data subject must be informed of this before giving consent [3].
- Article 7(2) also requires that consent requests in broader written declarations be clearly distinguishable, intelligible and in clear and plain language, with infringing parts not binding [4].

**Yes — the retailer's use is caught by the Article 5 prohibition; the purely scientific research use is not.**

- Article 5(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service, or using AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons in the workplace and education institutions, except where the system is intended for medical or safety reasons [1][2].
- The recitals explain this prohibition targets workplace/education emotion detection because of the power imbalance and intrusive nature of such systems [8], and note the exception covers systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, such as therapeutic use [3][8].
- However, the Regulation excludes from its scope AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development [6][7], so the lab's initial research-only use falls outside the Act.
- That exclusion is without prejudice to the obligation to comply with the Regulation where an AI system falling within its scope is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such research and development activity [5][6] — which is exactly what happens when the system is sold to the retailer.
- Once used by the retailer to monitor staff mood in shops, the system is used in the workplace for emotion inference, with no medical or safety justification, so it falls under the Article 5(f) prohibition [1][2].

Under Article 20, the platform must give the user access to an internal complaint-handling system for at least six months, starting from the day the user is informed of the decision, and complaints must be lodged electronically and free of charge. The system must be easy to access, user-friendly, and allow sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated complaints, which the platform must handle in a timely, non-discriminatory, diligent and non-arbitrary manner.

It had to notify within 2 months, and the maximum fine is 1% of total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year.

- Article 3(3) requires an undertaking meeting all thresholds in paragraph 2 to notify the Commission without delay and in any event within 2 months after the thresholds are met.
- Article 30 allows the Commission to impose fines not exceeding 1% of total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year where an undertaking intentionally or negligently fails to comply with the obligation to notify the Commission according to Article 3(3).

No, the short-term right to reject is no longer available.

- Under section 22(1) and (3), the short-term right to reject is lost if the 30-day time limit (beginning with the first day after ownership/possession transfer, delivery and any required installation) passes without it being exercised; ten weeks exceeds 30 days.
- The next remedy is the right to repair or replacement under section 23, which is one of the rights available under section 19(3) for goods not of satisfactory quality (a breach of the section 9 term).
- If repair or replacement fails (after one attempt), is impossible or disproportionate, or the trader breaches the requirement to act within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience, the consumer may then exercise the right to a price reduction or the final right to reject under section 24(5).
- On proof of when the fault arose: section 19(14) provides that goods not conforming at any time within six months of delivery are taken not to have conformed on the day of delivery, so the consumer does not have to prove the fault existed at delivery.
- This presumption does not apply if it is established the goods did conform on that day, or if applying it is incompatible with the nature of the goods or how they fail to conform (section 19(15)).

Digital Services Act - 45 million threshold: average monthly active recipients of the service in the Union equal to or higher than 45 million, equivalent to 10 % of the Union population, calculated as an average over a period of six months, for designation as very large online platforms or very large online search engines (Art. 33(1); recital).

Digital Markets Act - 45 million threshold: at least 45 million monthly active end users established or located in the Union in the last financial year, identified and calculated in accordance with the methodology and indicators set out in the Annex (Art. 3(1)(b)).

Digital Markets Act - additional requirement alongside the 45 million: at least 10 000 yearly active business users established in the Union, and the thresholds in point (b) must have been met in each of the last three financial years (Art. 3(1)(b) and (c)).

Both Acts use a 45 million monthly user figure, but the DSA counts average monthly active recipients of an online platform or search engine service (a six-month average, ~10 % of the Union population), while the DMA counts monthly active end users of a core platform service; the DMA additionally requires at least 10 000 yearly active business users and that the thresholds were met in each of the last three financial years.

Artificial Intelligence Act (prohibited AI practice, Art. 99(3)): 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover
Digital Services Act (Commission fine on very large online platform, Art. 74(1)): 6 % of total worldwide annual turnover
Digital Markets Act (Commission fine on gatekeeper, first offence, Art. 30(1)): 10 % of total worldwide annual turnover

Ranked from lowest to highest, the AI Act's 7 % exceeds the DSA's 6 %, while the DMA's 10 % for a first offence is the highest of the three.

The AI Act uses the GDPR definition: Article 3(50) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 defines 'personal data' as "personal data as defined in Article 4, point (1), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679." The same cross-reference is used for 'non-personal data' in Article 3(51), which means data other than that personal data.

AI Act (general case) - Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 73(2): not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident
GDPR - Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Art. 33(1): where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of the breach

The GDPR's 72-hour deadline is shorter than the AI Act's 15-day deadline (72 hours = 3 days vs 15 days).
